title: Arvi Teikari - Why Noita Became a Roguelite (and Why I Liked That a Lot)
speaker: Arvi Teikari
summary: Arvi Teikari recounts Noita's roughly eight-year development, during which the pixel-physics game was prototyped as an arcade arena platformer, a Terraria-like survival game, a god game, a space RTS, a sci-fi explorer and a Fallout-like open world before settling on a roguelite. He explains the recurring problems: pathfinding in a fully dynamic world, erratic randomness, showcasing pixel physics without everything being destroyed, making material reactions matter to gameplay, and the exploding workload of open-world ambitions. A roguelite framing solved many of these: randomness is expected, permadeath self-balances destruction, obscure interactions can be spread across many runs, single-character movement avoids AI problems, and progression becomes player knowledge. He closes by explaining the 'roguelite' label as a way to honor traditional roguelikes.

insights.claim: Noita simulates every pixel as a material that can react with others (fire ignites wood, water turns to steam and extinguishes fire), and this falling-sand simulation was the founding idea of the game.
insights.detail: Teikari describes Noita as a Spelunky-like roguelite platformer whose big selling point is the powder-toy-style pixel physics, a complicated and granular emergent system the whole game was built around.
insights.quote: the materials can interact with each other they can like there can be fire that can react with wood to lit the wood on fire

insights.claim: Noita's wand system, where spells placed in a wand's slots combine into new effects, is one of the game's three pillars alongside roguelite structure and pixel physics.
insights.detail: Introduced around 2014, the system lets magic wands hold spells in slots that combine. Teikari says it is hard to explain briefly but counts it as the third big thing in Noita.
insights.quote: you have magic wands that have slots and you put spells on those slots to combine different spells into new things

insights.claim: Noita spent years from 2012 to 2016 cycling through genres (arena platformer, Terraria-like survival, god game, space RTS, sci-fi explorer, post-apocalyptic open world) before committing to a roguelite.
insights.detail: The original idea came from Petri Purho's Bloody Zombies, a puzzle platformer about swimming in blood. Each subsequent concept had design issues, and the team gradually drifted toward the roguelite approach.
insights.quote: notice identity changed quite quite a lot over that 2012 to 2016 period

insights.claim: Noita chose a roguelite over an open world partly because a roguelite has a far more manageable scope after years without a clear idea of the game's scope.
insights.detail: At a design meeting deciding between open world and roguelite, the team favored roguelite for design reasons and because the term open world itself implies a large scope.
insights.quote: it felt like a roguelite would have a much more manageable scope than an open world adventure game

insights.claim: In a world where every pixel can move, robust and fast pathfinding for many AI agents (like a god game's tribe using ladders) proved maybe not impossible but too much, one of the design troubles that undermined Noita's early god-game concept.
insights.detail: Sand falling and water pouring constantly rearrange terrain. The team tried flying jet-pack characters to simplify pathfinding, then shelved AI for years before revisiting it in the roguelite phase. Of the later space RTS concept, Teikari says he doesn't remember its problems but they were probably similar.
insights.quote: making a robust uh pathfinding system that doesn't slow down hugely is not trivial

insights.claim: A highly dynamic simulation produces random accidents from bugs, AI and material reactions, making it hard to build a world that uses its dynamism well without feeling too erratic.
insights.detail: Teikari says the team fought this all the way through development; gameplay feedback was difficult when anything could happen anywhere.
insights.quote: it was difficult to create a game world that felt uh that utilized this dynamicness in a good way while not being too random too erratic

insights.claim: A fully destructible, seamlessly generated world clashes with 'gamey' structures like Spelunky's static transition rooms between freshly populated areas.
insights.detail: Because Noita grew out of open-world prototypes, it had a seamless continually generated world, and many systems the team tried struggled with everything being so dynamic.
insights.quote: we implemented like a seamless con continually generated world and that worked really badly with this concept of having this static more game-like transition areas

insights.claim: Letting players destroy everything is the easiest way to showcase a physics simulation but quickly becomes boring, because once everything is destroyed there is nothing left to see.
insights.detail: Unlimited destruction is either a constant danger to the player or a way to trivialize the game. In the first arena prototype, turning everything into acid was the most fun way to play but also the most boring, leaving each level a melted pile of garbage.
insights.quote: that's fun for a moment and it's a very easy system to showcase hey this is what we can do but it becomes boring very quickly

insights.claim: Many physically plausible material reactions (ice freezing, sand pouring, fungal soil sprouting) are interesting in themselves but hard to turn into meaningful gameplay decisions.
insights.detail: Wood burning is easily gamified, but the team constantly had to ask how players would actually see and meaningfully use the cool things simulated behind the scenes, beyond simple interactions like hardening lava with water.
insights.quote: only a very small part of them very small kind of set of them were immediately interesting from a gameplay perspective

insights.claim: Open-world ambitions on top of a dynamic emergent simulation cause exponential workload and feature creep, as shown by Noita's abandoned sword-casting blacksmith system.
insights.detail: The idea was to dig a sword-shaped hole, pour molten metal and get a recognized sword, but even digging one-pixel holes in a fully simulated world without it being annoying was a huge hassle. Keeping the team sane over eight years became a design problem.
insights.quote: the workload increases exponentially very quickly when you start working on a open world thing with so much dynamicness

insights.claim: Permadeath made Noita's destructive powers self-balancing: players get powerful destruction but can easily kill themselves, and dying hilariously is part of the fun.
insights.detail: A roguelite carries the assumption of random factors, good and bad luck, and challenging bad situations or dying. That reframed destruction from a balance problem into a feature.
insights.quote: because of the permadeath you could easily kill yourself and that was kind of part of the idea of the game so the destruction suddenly was kind of self-balancing

insights.claim: Even while accepting randomness, the Noita team actively limited instant-kill situations, tracking each addition's effect on 'insta-kill cleanliness' on an office design board.
insights.detail: The board listed pluses and minuses of different additions and how they affected the chance of being screwed over by a random thing.
insights.quote: we definitely spent a lot of time time trying to limit insta kill things where you can just like get screwed over by a random thing

insights.claim: Because roguelite players do many runs, rare and obscure interactions can be hidden in the world and discovered over time, making the game feel mysterious when players share finds.
insights.detail: Not having to show everything in one run let Noita include obscure material reactions that turn up rarely; a player who tries something random and sees something new reports it to others.
insights.quote: also there's the bonus of not having to show everything on a single run we could hide a lot of things in the game world

insights.claim: The roguelite framing cut Noita's scope by removing whole problem areas: only one player character's movement needed solving, and base building and shaped digging were dropped.
insights.detail: The team no longer needed player-controlled AI agents or pixel-precise digging; it concentrated on platforming and going deeper.
insights.quote: we only had to solve the movement for a single character that you control

insights.claim: Roguelite players are expected to experiment, so a deep system like Noita's wand building can leave its depth for players (or wikis) to find, which also reduced the team's workload.
insights.detail: Teikari calls this maybe controversial, but the assumption that players find the depth themselves let the team avoid explaining everything.
insights.quote: there's the assumption of the player having to do some experimentation we could maybe include some things that require the player to experiment

insights.claim: Noita relies on 'virtual skill': instead of unlocking more powerful items over time, players progress by increasing their knowledge, which suits dynamic emergent systems.
insights.detail: The team considered this a lot during development as an alternative to unlocks and ever-increasing destruction on every run.
insights.quote: on every run you increase your knowledge of the game and that works really well with the like dynamicness and emergent systems

insights.claim: Noita calls itself a roguelite rather than a roguelike to honor traditional ASCII, turn-based, top-down roguelikes and distinguish itself from them.
insights.detail: The team was aware of NetHack, Dungeon Crawl, ADOM, Angband and IVAN and wanted to separate those from action games like Spelunky and Binding of Isaac.
insights.quote: we kind of wanted to underline this difference between uh ascii graphics turn based permadeath uh top-down roguelikes
